title: How many days does an albatross take to cross an ocean?
description: A trip of twelve thousand kilometres is divided by the distance flown each day, once for the fastest day and once for the slowest day. The two answers give a range of days, and each end is checked by multiplying back.
teaching_notes: One idea: days equal the distance divided by the distance flown each day, so a range of daily distances gives a range of days. Watch for students who round thirteen and a bit down to thirteen, when the bird is still flying on the fourteenth day.

source: Grey-headed albatrosses have a roughly 7-feet wide wingspan. They are known to migrate across several oceans. Albatrosses can cover about 900 to 1000 km in a day. One of the longest single trips recorded is about 12,000 km. How many days would such a trip take to cross an ocean approximately?
video_script.why: The child divides a long distance by a distance for one day, and now does it for a range of daily distances to get a range of days.
video_script.substitution: Divide the trip distance by the fastest and by the slowest distance flown each day, and read the two answers as a range.
video_script.anchor: a grey-headed albatross over an ocean, with the trip of 12,000 km marked along the water
video_script.payoff_line: Divide the distance by the distance flown each day, once for each speed
maths_rules: days = distance / distance flown each day
at 900 km each day: 12,000 / 900 = 13.33 days, a little more than 13, so the trip runs into the 14th day
video_script.design: One idea: a range of daily distances gives a range of days. The albatross and the trip stay in the anchor band; the working band shows the two divisions and the checks. No hard clear.
open_questions: The exact range is 12 to 13.33 days; the worklist and the book say about 12 to 14 days. The video follows the book and explains that thirteen and a bit days runs into the fourteenth day.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>A grey-headed albatross has a wingspan of about seven feet, and it migrates across oceans.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>It can cover about nine hundred to one thousand kilometres in a day.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>One of its longest trips recorded is about twelve thousand kilometres.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>About how many days would such a trip take to cross an ocean?

beats.on_screen: the anchor holds still; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: cards: days = distance / distance flown each day; a faster bird needs fewer days; try the fastest and the slowest day

marks.m1: the card days = distance / distance flown each day appears
marks.m2: the card a faster bird needs fewer days appears
marks.m3: the card try the fastest and the slowest day appears

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>The days needed are the whole distance divided by the distance flown each day.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>A faster bird needs fewer days, and a slower bird needs more.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>We try the fastest day and the slowest day, which gives a range.

beats.on_screen: Given: trip 12,000 km; 900 to 1000 km each day

marks.m1: the given line is written in the working band

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, a trip of twelve thousand kilometres, flown at nine hundred to one thousand kilometres each day.

beats.on_screen: To find: about how many days the trip takes

marks.m1: the find line is written under the given line

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to find about how many days the trip takes.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: fastest day, 1000 km each day: 12,000 / 1000 = 12 days
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, take the fastest speed of one thousand kilometres each day.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Twelve thousand divided by one thousand is twelve.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The fastest trip takes twelve days.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: slowest day, 900 km each day: 12,000 / 900 = 13 and a bit; 13 days cover 13 x 900 = 11,700 km; 300 km are left, so part of a 14th day

marks.m3: 13 x 900 = 11,700 km is written, with 300 km left
marks.m4: the words part of a 14th day appear

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, take the slowest speed of nine hundred kilometres each day.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Twelve thousand divided by nine hundred is a little more than thirteen.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>After thirteen days the bird has flown eleven thousand seven hundred kilometres, so three hundred more are left.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Those last three hundred kilometres need part of a fourteenth day.

marks.m1: the heading check both ends appears
marks.m2: 12 x 1000 = 12,000 is written with a tick
marks.m3: 13 x 900 = 11,700 is written with the word short
marks.m4: 14 x 900 = 12,600 is written with the word enough

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, check both ends.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Twelve days at one thousand kilometres each day make exactly twelve thousand.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Thirteen days at nine hundred make eleven thousand seven hundred, which falls short.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Fourteen days at nine hundred make twelve thousand six hundred, which is enough.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Divide the distance by the distance flown each day, once for each speed.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The trip takes about twelve to fourteen days.
